messages.content: I want to develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation while generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity. I have two quantitative requirements: the maximum cellwise mass-balance error must stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, and, on unseen channel connectivity, breakthrough-time error must remain below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

That sets out two distinct requirements for the surrogate. The conservation requirement concerns the worst cellwise mass-balance error, not merely an aggregate error over the domain: at each timestep, that maximum must be less than 0.1% of the mass injected during that timestep. The generalization requirement concerns breakthrough timing when the channel connectivity is unseen, using a converged finite-volume solver as the comparison; the error must be below 5%. Both matter to the stated goal, and satisfying one would not by itself establish the other.
Can you unpack why the word “cellwise” matters here?

“Cellwise” makes the conservation requirement local. A small domain-wide discrepancy would not be enough to demonstrate it, because errors in different cells could offset each other when summed. The specified quantity is the maximum mass-balance error among cells, so the requirement constrains the worst cell rather than an average or a total. The threshold remains below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep.
So it would be misleading to say that good total mass balance alone meets the goal?

Yes. Good total mass balance may be relevant, but it does not establish the stated local criterion. To assess that criterion, the cellwise mass-balance errors have to be considered before taking their maximum. The requirement is that this maximum stays below 0.1% of the injected mass for the timestep in question.
What does “per timestep” add to the interpretation?

It makes the conservation bound a timestep-by-timestep requirement rather than a statement about a run considered only as a whole. For a given timestep, let the injected mass be M. The maximum cellwise mass-balance error for that timestep must then be less than 0.001M. That symbolic expression is just another way to state 0.1% of injected mass per timestep; it does not specify a particular timestep size or injection amount.
And “below” means the threshold is strict, not approximately equal to it?

As written, yes: below 0.1% is a strict bound. A reported maximum of exactly 0.1% would not be below 0.1%. The same wording applies to the breakthrough-time requirement: its error must remain below 5%, not simply reach 5%.
I also want to be clear about the generalization part. Is it just a request for accurate predictions on any new case?

It is more specific than that. The stated generalization condition is unseen permeability connectivity, with breakthrough-time accuracy called out on unseen channel connectivity. The requirement is not merely that some overall prediction score look good on new cases; it singles out the breakthrough-time error under that connectivity condition and compares it with a converged finite-volume solver.
Why keep the connectivity condition explicit instead of just saying “unseen permeability”?

Because the wording identifies connectivity as the aspect that must generalize. Saying only “unseen permeability” could be read more broadly or as a different kind of change in the permeability description. Keeping “unseen channel connectivity” in the breakthrough-time requirement preserves the particular condition under which the below-5% comparison is required.
How should I describe the finite-volume solver’s role without overstating it?

Describe it as the reference for the breakthrough-time comparison: on unseen channel connectivity, the surrogate’s breakthrough-time error must be below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver. “Converged” is part of the specified reference. The statement does not, by itself, give the solver configuration, define breakthrough, or assert that a comparison has already been performed.
Does the reference solver also define the cellwise conservation threshold?

Not in the wording given. The conservation threshold is expressed relative to injected mass per timestep: the maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of that mass. The converged finite-volume solver is explicitly named for the breakthrough-time comparison. Keeping those roles separate avoids recasting the local conservation requirement as an error relative to the solver.
Could a surrogate satisfy the breakthrough condition while failing local conservation?

Conceptually, yes. A breakthrough time could be close to the converged finite-volume result while a cell has a mass-balance error at or above the specified bound. Conversely, small cellwise mass-balance errors alone would not establish breakthrough-time accuracy on unseen channel connectivity. Those are illustrations of why the two stated requirements need to be assessed separately, not claims about any particular surrogate.
What, if anything, does this goal say about how the surrogate should be built?

It specifies the desired behavior and two performance bounds, but not an architecture, training procedure, or particular mechanism for enforcing conservation. Whatever approach is developed would need to preserve local mass conservation to the stated cellwise threshold and generalize sufficiently on unseen channel connectivity to meet the breakthrough-time comparison. The goal leaves the implementation open.
Would it be accurate to call the conservation requirement an average over all cells and timesteps?

No. That would weaken the stated requirement. “Maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep” calls for the maximum across cells to remain under the bound at each timestep. An average across cells or timesteps could conceal a cell or timestep that exceeds it.
Then give me a concise way to state the target without dropping the conditions.

Develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation and generalizes across unseen permeability connectivity: at every timestep, its maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of injected mass for that timestep, and on unseen channel connectivity its breakthrough-time error remains below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

For that subsurface two-phase flow surrogate, I’m considering a permeability-conditioned graph network that predicts transmissibility corrections. After that, I would solve for pressure and update saturations using shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes.

That is a proposed sequence: train the graph network to predict transmissibility corrections conditioned on permeability, then solve pressure and use shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes to update saturations. It separates what the network predicts from the pressure and saturation calculations. It is a proposed approach, not yet a result showing that the conservation or unseen-connectivity requirements are met.
What is the network predicting in that description?

Transmissibility corrections. Transmissibility describes how flow is conveyed between connected cells in a discretized flow calculation; the proposed network would predict corrections to that quantity. The description does not say that the network directly predicts pressure, saturation, or breakthrough time.
And what does “permeability-conditioned” contribute?

It says the predicted corrections depend on permeability information. That is pertinent to the aim of generalizing across permeability connectivity, but it does not specify exactly how permeability is represented or supplied to the graph network. Nor does conditioning alone establish that the predictions will generalize to unseen channel connectivity.
I don’t want the phrase “graph network” to imply an architecture I haven’t chosen. How narrowly can we read it?

Here, it identifies the proposed kind of predictive model: a graph network trained to output transmissibility corrections. The node does not specify its layers, graph construction, input features beyond permeability conditioning, or training targets. Those details should remain open rather than being treated as decisions already made.
Why distinguish transmissibility corrections from just predicting the flow state?

Because the proposal gives the network a particular role within a larger calculation. Its stated output is a correction to transmissibility; pressure is then solved, and saturation is updated using finite-volume phase fluxes. Describing the surrogate as a direct pressure-and-saturation predictor would omit that division of roles and change what the proposal says.
Does “then solve pressure” mean the pressure calculation is still part of the surrogate workflow?

Yes. In this proposal, training the network does not replace the subsequent pressure solve. The intended workflow uses the network’s transmissibility corrections and then solves for pressure before updating saturations. The description does not specify the pressure solver or the equations used in that solve.
Could you clarify “shared-face” without claiming that the approach has already passed the mass-balance test?

In a finite-volume calculation, neighboring cells meet at a common face. Using a shared-face phase flux means accounting for the same face flux consistently for the cells on either side, with opposite signs in their respective balances. That is a structural way to avoid assigning two incompatible flux values to one internal face. It supports local flux accounting, but it is not, by itself, evidence that the specified maximum cellwise mass-balance error has been achieved.
Why say “phase fluxes” in the plural?

The proposal concerns two-phase flow, so the finite-volume flux accounting is phase-specific. “Shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes” keeps both aspects explicit: the fluxes are used across shared faces, and they are fluxes for the phases. The proposal does not give a formula for calculating them.
Is the saturation update just another prediction from the graph network?

Not as stated. The graph network is trained to predict transmissibility corrections; saturations are updated afterward using the shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes. Calling saturation a direct network output would describe a different proposal.
Can I claim that using a shared flux automatically guarantees my local mass-conservation threshold?

No. Sharing a face flux allows contributions at an internal face to be accounted for consistently between neighboring cells. Whether the full calculation meets the cellwise mass-balance bound also depends on the complete pressure and saturation updates and their accounting of mass. The proposal specifies a conservation-oriented structure, not a verified maximum error below the threshold.
Likewise, does permeability conditioning guarantee the breakthrough-time requirement on unseen channel connectivity?

No. It makes permeability relevant to the network’s predicted transmissibility corrections, but the required breakthrough-time accuracy on unseen channel connectivity remains something to assess against the converged finite-volume solver. Neither the conditioning nor the proposed calculation sequence establishes that error bound in advance.
How would you state the whole idea while keeping the prediction and calculation stages distinct?

Train a permeability-conditioned graph network to predict transmissibility corrections; then solve pressure and update saturations using shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes. That wording states the proposed method without implying that training is complete, specifying unchosen implementation details, or claiming that either performance requirement has already been met.

My hypothesis is that shared-face fluxes will keep the cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per step, while graph-conditioned transmissibility corrections will keep breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity.

That is a two-part hypothesis about the proposed surrogate, not an observed result. The shared-face fluxes are expected to keep the maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass at each timestep. Separately, the graph-conditioned corrections are expected to keep breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity, versus a converged finite-volume solver. Each expectation corresponds to a different part of the goal.
Why phrase the first part as the maximum cellwise error rather than simply “cellwise error”?

The stated requirement concerns the worst cell: the maximum cellwise mass-balance error must stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. Saying only “cellwise error” could leave unclear whether the hypothesis applies to every cell or merely to some representative value. Referring to the maximum makes the intended bound explicit.
What is the reasoning behind expecting shared-face fluxes to help with that?

A shared-face finite-volume flux gives neighboring cells a consistent value to account for at their common face, with opposite signs in their respective balances. That is a reason to expect more consistent local mass accounting than if the two sides used incompatible values. It does not, on its own, establish the numerical bound: the claim that the maximum cellwise imbalance stays below 0.1% of injected mass per step remains a hypothesis.
So should I say the shared-face construction guarantees the 0.1% bound?

No. The hypothesis says shared-face fluxes *keep* the imbalance below that bound; it has not established a guarantee. The shared-face construction explains why the expectation is plausible, but the specified maximum error is a quantitative condition on the full calculation. Keeping those statements distinct avoids presenting the hypothesis as a measured or proven outcome.
Does “per step” mean I could average imbalance over the run and compare that average with 0.1%?

No. It means the bound applies at each timestep, using the injected mass for that timestep as the reference. The relevant quantity is the maximum error across cells for that step. An average over steps could fall below 0.1% even if a particular step exceeded the bound, so it would not express this hypothesis accurately.
Let me check the other half: is the graph network supposed to predict breakthrough time directly?

Not in the proposed approach. The permeability-conditioned graph network predicts transmissibility corrections; pressure is then solved and saturations are updated using shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes. The hypothesis is that the graph-conditioned corrections, as part of that workflow, keep the resulting breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity. It does not turn breakthrough time into a direct network output.
Why connect the breakthrough claim specifically to the graph-conditioned corrections?

That is the causal expectation expressed by the hypothesis: corrections conditioned on permeability are expected to help the surrogate retain breakthrough-time accuracy when channel connectivity is unseen. It is an expectation about how that part of the proposal will contribute, not evidence that the corrections already achieve the below-5% result.
Should “unseen connectivity” be left broad, or should I retain “unseen channel connectivity”?

Retain “unseen channel connectivity” when stating the breakthrough-time bound. The broader goal concerns generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity, but the quantitative breakthrough requirement names unseen channel connectivity in particular. That qualifier says where the below-5% error is expected to hold.
And the 5% is relative to what?

The comparison is with a converged finite-volume solver. The hypothesis is that, on unseen channel connectivity, breakthrough-time error versus that reference remains below 5%. Without the reference, “below 5%” would leave the comparison unspecified.
Could the two parts of the hypothesis be collapsed into one claim that the surrogate works?

That would lose important distinctions. One part concerns local mass-balance error, measured cell by cell against injected mass per timestep; the other concerns breakthrough-time error on unseen channel connectivity, compared with a converged finite-volume solver. A general statement that the surrogate “works” would not preserve either quantitative bound or the conditions attached to it.
Does the hypothesis say that good local balance causes good breakthrough timing?

No. It assigns the local-imbalance expectation to shared-face fluxes and the unseen-connectivity breakthrough expectation to graph-conditioned corrections. It does not claim that meeting the mass-balance bound causes the breakthrough-time bound, or that either one follows automatically from the other.
If one of the two bounds were met, would that establish the whole hypothesis?

No. The hypothesis makes both claims. Showing the maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per step would address its conservation part, but not the below-5% breakthrough-time error on unseen channel connectivity. Likewise, breakthrough-time accuracy alone would not establish the local imbalance claim.
Can you put it in one sentence that still sounds explicitly hypothetical?

We hypothesize that shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes will keep the maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, and that graph-conditioned transmissibility corrections will keep breakthrough-time error below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity.

To evaluate the hypothesis, I want to benchmark 200 held-out channel-connectivity realizations against converged finite-volume solutions. I would measure the maximum per-step injected-mass-normalized cellwise imbalance and the breakthrough-time error.

That benchmark addresses both parts of the hypothesis. The 200 held-out channel-connectivity realizations provide cases for assessing behavior on connectivity not used in training. For each case, the local-conservation measure is the maximum cellwise imbalance at each step, normalized by the mass injected during that step. Breakthrough-time error is assessed against the converged finite-volume solution. This describes the planned evaluation; it does not yet say what either measure will be.
Can you clarify what “200 held-out” commits us to saying?

It specifies the number and status of the benchmark cases: 200 channel-connectivity realizations are held out for evaluation. It does not specify how they were generated, what their channel patterns look like, or how the training cases were selected. The important condition here is that the benchmark tests held-out channel connectivity rather than reporting only on cases used for training.
I don’t want “200” mistaken for the number of timesteps.

Then keep it attached to “held-out channel-connectivity realizations.” There are 200 realizations in the proposed benchmark; “per-step” describes how the mass-imbalance measure is formed within a realization. The node does not state a number of timesteps.
What exactly is maximized in the conservation measure?

At a given timestep, the cellwise mass imbalances are considered and the maximum is taken across cells. That worst-cell imbalance is normalized by the injected mass for that step. This preserves the local nature of the requirement: an average over cells would not reveal whether an individual cell exceeded the 0.1% threshold.
Does the phrase “injected-mass-normalized” change the denominator from step to step?

The stated measure uses injected mass per step, so each step’s cellwise imbalance is judged relative to the mass injected during that step. It should not be silently replaced with a whole-run injection total or with an average injected mass across steps. The benchmark description does not provide particular injection amounts.
Could I instead report one average imbalance across all 200 cases?

An average could be additional information, but it would not replace the stated measure or assess the worst-cell bound on its own. The benchmark calls for maximum per-step injected-mass-normalized cellwise imbalance. Averaging across cases, cells, or steps could hide an exceedance of the below-0.1%-of-injected-mass-per-timestep requirement.
How do the converged finite-volume solutions enter the comparison?

They provide the benchmark reference, particularly for breakthrough-time error: the surrogate’s breakthrough timing on each held-out channel-connectivity realization is compared with that of the corresponding converged finite-volume solution. The activity says to benchmark against those solutions; it does not give their numerical results or specify solver settings.
Should I describe the cellwise imbalance as a breakthrough-time difference from the solver too?

No. Those are different measurements. Cellwise imbalance is a local mass-balance quantity normalized by injected mass per step. Breakthrough-time error concerns the difference in breakthrough timing relative to a converged finite-volume solution. Putting both into the same benchmark does not make them the same kind of error.
Is the below-5% condition an average over the 200 realizations?

The stated goal is that breakthrough-time error remains below 5% on unseen channel connectivity versus a converged finite-volume solver. The benchmarking activity says to measure that error on 200 held-out realizations; it does not introduce an average-error criterion. An average below 5% alone would not show that the error remains below 5% across the held-out cases.
And for conservation, is a single worst step enough to describe what happened?

The maximum over steps could be a compact way to report the worst per-step value, provided it comes from the specified cellwise measure. But the underlying condition is per timestep: at each step, take the maximum across cells and compare it with 0.1% of that step’s injected mass. The activity does not prescribe a reporting format.
What does this benchmark test about the graph-conditioned corrections specifically?

It tests the prediction associated with them: whether the resulting surrogate keeps breakthrough-time error below 5% on held-out channel connectivity when compared with converged finite-volume solutions. The benchmark measures the outcome of the proposed workflow; the activity does not, by itself, isolate the corrections’ contribution from every other part of that workflow.
What does it test about shared-face fluxes?

It tests the associated local-balance prediction by measuring the maximum per-step injected-mass-normalized cellwise imbalance. Shared-face fluxes motivate the hypothesis, but the measured imbalance is what would indicate whether the stated quantitative bound holds in these benchmark cases. The planned measurement is not itself a result.
Could I say the benchmark will demonstrate that both bounds hold?

Not before the measurements are available. You can say the benchmark is designed to evaluate whether the maximum cellwise imbalance stays below 0.1% of injected mass per step and whether breakthrough-time error stays below 5% against converged finite-volume solutions on the held-out channel-connectivity realizations. Whether either bound actually holds is an outcome, not part of the activity as stated.
Can you give me a clean description of the evaluation without adding a solver configuration or a breakthrough definition?

Benchmark the surrogate on 200 held-out channel-connectivity realizations against converged finite-volume solutions, measuring the maximum cellwise mass imbalance normalized by injected mass at each step and the breakthrough-time error relative to the corresponding finite-volume solution. Use those measurements to evaluate the local-conservation and unseen-connectivity breakthrough hypotheses; do not assume either threshold has already been met.
The benchmark results are in. Across 200 held-out channel realizations, the maximum per-step normalized cellwise imbalance was 0.06%, and the worst-case breakthrough-time error was 4.2%.

Those are two reported extremes from the 200 held-out channel realizations. The 0.06% figure is the maximum reported cellwise mass imbalance when normalized by injected mass per step. The 4.2% figure is the worst reported breakthrough-time error, with breakthrough timing compared against the converged finite-volume solutions used in the benchmark. Neither number is an average across realizations.
Could you unpack what the 0.06% result represents?

The measurement starts with cellwise mass imbalance at each step and uses the injected mass for that step as the normalization. “Maximum” identifies the largest value reported across the benchmark, rather than a typical cell’s imbalance. The result is 0.06%; it does not identify which cell, step, or held-out realization produced that value.
Does that mean every cell had an imbalance of 0.06%?

No. A maximum does not say that all cells had the same imbalance. It reports the uppermost observed value of the specified per-step normalized cellwise measure across the 200 held-out realizations. The result alone does not provide the values for the other cells or steps.
I want to keep the denominator clear. Is 0.06% a percentage of the total mass injected over the whole benchmark?

No. The measure is normalized by injected mass per step. The 0.06% result is reported for that per-step-normalized cellwise imbalance measure, not as a fraction of the total mass injected across all steps or all 200 realizations.
And how should I read “worst-case” for the 4.2% figure?

It identifies the largest breakthrough-time error reported among the held-out channel realizations in this benchmark. It does not mean every realization had a 4.2% error, and it does not give the average, median, or spread of breakthrough-time errors.
What is the breakthrough-time error compared with?

The benchmark compares the held-out realizations against converged finite-volume solutions, so those solutions are the reference for the breakthrough-time error. The reported worst-case error is 4.2%. The result does not state the breakthrough times themselves or identify the realization with that worst-case error.
Are the two percentages interchangeable measures of the same thing?

No. Although both are percentages, 0.06% describes a mass-balance quantity: the maximum cellwise imbalance normalized by injected mass per step. The 4.2% describes error in breakthrough time relative to the converged finite-volume reference. Their different denominators and meanings matter more than their shared percentage notation.
Could I say which realization produced both extremes?

Not from these results. They give the maximum imbalance and the worst-case breakthrough-time error across the 200 held-out channel realizations, but do not identify either realization. The two extremes need not be attributed to the same case without that information.
Do these figures show that the shared-face fluxes, on their own, caused the imbalance result?

The figures report an outcome of the benchmarked surrogate; they do not isolate the effect of shared-face fluxes. The 0.06% measurement is informative about local balance in the evaluated runs, but the result as stated does not establish a separate causal contribution from one part of the workflow.
Is the same caution appropriate for the graph-conditioned corrections and the breakthrough result?

Yes. The 4.2% worst-case error describes breakthrough-time performance on the held-out channel realizations relative to converged finite-volume solutions. It does not, by itself, measure how much of that outcome is attributable specifically to the graph-conditioned transmissibility corrections.
What does “held-out” let me say about the scope of the evidence?

It lets you identify the evaluated set as 200 channel realizations held out from training, rather than cases used to train the surrogate. The reported maxima describe that evaluated set. The figures do not provide results for every possible unseen channel connectivity or for a different collection of realizations.
Can I infer a distribution of errors from the two reported extremes?

No. The two extremes do not tell us how values are distributed below them. For example, the results do not state how many realizations were near the worst-case breakthrough-time error or how per-step cellwise imbalances varied through the runs. Reporting a mean or a pattern from these figures alone would add information that is not present.
Give me a concise results sentence that preserves both measurements and the benchmark reference.

Across 200 held-out channel-connectivity realizations benchmarked against converged finite-volume solutions, the maximum per-step injected-mass-normalized cellwise imbalance was 0.06%, and the worst-case breakthrough-time error was 4.2%.
Can permeability-conditioned graph corrections resolve unseen dead-end channels adjacent to injection wells at 100:1 permeability contrast?

That is an open capability question. The proposed graph network predicts transmissibility corrections conditioned on permeability, but the proposal alone does not establish whether those corrections capture an unseen dead-end channel beside an injection well at 100:1 permeability contrast. “Resolve” also needs care: it could mean distinguishing that terminating channel in the corrected flow calculation, or it could mean obtaining accurate downstream predictions. Neither outcome is given here.
What is the distinctive feature of a dead-end channel in this question?

Its connectivity terminates rather than continuing as a throughgoing channel. The question asks whether the corrections can account for that feature when it was unseen, not merely whether they respond to a permeability contrast. It does not specify the channel’s shape, length, or precise connection to the well.
Does “adjacent to injection wells” mean the channel must be connected to a well?

Not necessarily. “Adjacent” establishes proximity to injection wells, but it does not specify a direct connection, a shared face, or where the channel ends relative to a well. Those details should not be assumed when stating the question.
Why does the 100:1 contrast belong in the wording?

It fixes the permeability-contrast condition under which the capability is being asked about. Without it, the question would cover an unspecified range of contrasts. A ratio of 100:1 identifies the magnitude of the contrast, but the wording does not say which region has which permeability or give absolute permeability values.
Should I read that as a 100:1 contrast between the channel and its surroundings?

The question names a 100:1 permeability contrast in the setting of unseen dead-end channels, but does not explicitly identify the two regions being compared. Describing it simply as the specified 100:1 contrast preserves the condition without assigning the higher or lower permeability to a particular region.
Is the word “unseen” about new injection wells or new channel connectivity?

Here it qualifies the dead-end channels: the question is whether the permeability-conditioned corrections can resolve that unseen connectivity pattern. It does not say that the injection wells themselves are new or that their locations have changed.
What would be too strong an answer to my question right now?

An unqualified “yes, the corrections resolve these channels” would claim an outcome not provided. An unqualified “no, they cannot” would be just as unsupported. The proposal identifies what the network predicts, while this question asks whether those predictions are adequate for a particular unseen channel configuration and contrast.
Could I at least say permeability conditioning makes the network aware of the 100:1 contrast?

You can say the corrections are conditioned on permeability, so permeability information is relevant to what the network predicts. But the description does not specify how that information is represented or whether it lets the network distinguish a dead end adjacent to an injection well at 100:1 contrast. Conditioning is not the same as demonstrating that capability.
Does predicting transmissibility corrections mean the graph network directly draws the dead-end channel?

No. Its stated output is transmissibility corrections, not a channel map. The question is whether those corrections can adequately reflect the unseen dead-end connectivity in the subsequent flow calculation. It does not prescribe a separate channel-identification output.
Does the pressure solve settle the question automatically?

No. In the proposed workflow, pressure is solved after the corrections are predicted, and saturations are then updated using shared-face finite-volume phase fluxes. Performing those steps does not, by itself, tell us whether the corrections represent this particular unseen dead-end configuration adequately.
Is this asking only whether the channel’s end is recognized, rather than whether the resulting flow is right?

“Resolve” leaves that distinction open. Recognizing that a channel terminates is one possible interpretation; representing its effect in the calculated pressure, phase fluxes, or saturation update is another. The question does not define an accuracy measure for this specific configuration, so it is better not to substitute one interpretation silently for the other.
Would a model that reacts to high permeability everywhere necessarily distinguish a dead end from a connected path?

Not necessarily. The issue posed is connectivity, not only the magnitude of permeability. The question specifically asks about an unseen *dead-end* channel adjacent to injection wells under the stated contrast. Merely responding to contrast would not, on its own, answer whether the terminating connectivity is resolved.
Can we say anything definite about the wells’ role?

Only that the dead-end channels in question are adjacent to injection wells. The wording does not specify well placement within a cell, injection conditions, or a particular interaction between a well and a channel. Those would add details beyond the question.
Should I treat this as a statement that the graph corrections fail at 100:1?
No. It is phrased as a question about whether they *can* resolve that configuration. It neither reports failure nor reports success at 100:1 permeability contrast.
Could you restate it without implying an answer or inventing a test?

The open question is whether permeability-conditioned graph-predicted transmissibility corrections can adequately represent unseen dead-end channels adjacent to injection wells when the permeability contrast is 100:1. The question specifies the configuration and contrast, but does not establish the outcome or define a separate resolution criterion.
I’d like to use the 200-realization benchmark as a baseline, then test added near-well dead ends at 100:1 permeability contrast against finite-volume breakthrough and mass-balance metrics.

That is a plan to examine the specific open question about unseen dead-end channels adjacent to injection wells. The existing 200-realization benchmark serves as the baseline; the added near-well dead ends at 100:1 contrast are the condition to test. Breakthrough and mass-balance metrics, with finite-volume solutions as the benchmark reference, would show how the surrogate performs under that added condition. The plan does not yet report an outcome.
What does calling the 200-realization benchmark a baseline mean here?

It means using that benchmark as the point of comparison for the added near-well dead-end test. It does not mean the 200 realizations themselves are all near-well dead ends, or that the planned test has already been carried out. The plan does not specify how many added cases there will be.
Should I say the 100:1 cases replace the original 200 realizations?

No. “Using the 200-realization benchmark as baseline” and “test added 100:1 near-well dead ends” distinguish the baseline from the added condition. The wording does not specify whether the added cases are modifications of benchmark cases or a separate set, so it is best not to claim either arrangement.
What exactly is the new condition this plan focuses on?

Dead-end channels near injection wells under a 100:1 permeability contrast. That focuses the test on the connectivity feature raised in the question: a channel that terminates rather than continuing through. The plan does not give its geometry, its exact relationship to a well, or which region has the higher permeability.
Would “near-well” let me say a dead end is directly connected to an injection well?

No. “Near-well” conveys proximity; the open question identifies injection wells as the nearby wells. Direct connection is a more specific condition that the plan does not state. You can preserve the intended setting by saying “dead ends near injection wells” without specifying a connection.
Why retain the 100:1 ratio in the test description?

It is the specified permeability-contrast condition for this test. Omitting it would make the plan sound like a test of near-well dead ends at any contrast. The ratio does not, on its own, provide absolute permeability values or identify which part of the configuration has the higher permeability.
How does the plan address whether the graph corrections resolve the dead ends?

It proposes checking the surrogate’s behavior in the added dead-end condition through breakthrough and mass-balance metrics against finite-volume results. That can provide evidence relevant to the question, but the plan does not define a separate channel-resolution metric or claim that the corrections themselves have been isolated as the cause of any outcome.
Should breakthrough and mass balance be treated as a single score?

Not as stated. They concern different aspects of the flow calculation. Breakthrough measures the timing outcome relative to the finite-volume reference, while mass balance concerns local accounting of mass. Keeping both metrics visible makes clear what the added near-well condition is being tested against without inventing a combined score.
Can I carry over the per-step, cellwise interpretation for mass balance?

Yes, as the mass-balance metric of the baseline benchmark: maximum cellwise imbalance normalized by injected mass per step. Identifying that metric makes the planned comparison understandable. It does not mean the added dead-end test has already produced a mass-balance value.
And is the finite-volume comparison about breakthrough time specifically?

Breakthrough time is the stated breakthrough metric, compared with a converged finite-volume solution in the benchmark. The plan also calls for mass-balance metrics. Those should remain distinct: a cellwise mass imbalance normalized by injected mass per step is not itself a breakthrough-time difference from the solver.
Could I describe the plan as proving the corrections will handle 100:1 dead ends?

No. It proposes a test of that capability. The added cases and their finite-volume comparisons have not been reported here, so the plan cannot establish that the permeability-conditioned graph corrections resolve the dead ends or that they fail to do so.
Do I need to specify how many added dead-end cases there are?
